trust: The Library of Congress is a taxpayer trust: held in trust for the people who paid for it, not a government organization or entity.
s: The American Revolution was the fight that made the United States a free country.
Colonists were angry about taxes they had no say in.
In 1775 fighting began at Lexington and Concord in Massachusetts.
George Washington led the Continental Army.
With help from France, the Americans won the war.
In 1783 Great Britain agreed that the United States was independent.
After the French and Indian War, Parliament taxed the colonies through measures such as the Stamp Act (1765) and the Townshend Acts, and colonists protested "no taxation without representation."
Tensions led to the Boston Massacre (1770), the Boston Tea Party (1773), and the punishing Coercive Acts.
Fighting began at Lexington and Concord on April 19, 1775, and the Second Continental Congress named George Washington commander of the Continental Army.
The American victory at Saratoga in 1777 persuaded France to enter an alliance in 1778, and French troops and ships helped trap the British army at Yorktown in 1781.
The Treaty of Paris of 1783 recognized American independence.
Militias, soldiers, and civilians of many backgrounds fought, and the war's ideals of liberty and self-government shaped the new nation's constitutions.
Ancient Egypt grew up along the Nile River in Africa.
Every year the river flooded and left rich soil for farming.
They built huge pyramids as tombs.
Egyptians wrote with pictures called hieroglyphs.
They also made paper from a plant called papyrus.
Egyptian civilization united under one king around 3100 BCE and lasted, with interruptions, until Rome conquered it in 30 BCE.
Life depended on the Nile's yearly flood, which deposited silt for farming; Egyptians measured the flood and built canals to manage it.
Historians divide the history into the Old, Middle, and New Kingdoms.
The Great Pyramid of Giza was built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BCE.
Scribes wrote in hieroglyphic and simpler scripts on papyrus, and the Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, helped scholars decipher hieroglyphs in 1822.
Egyptians made advances in geometry, medicine, and calendar keeping, and their belief in an afterlife shaped tombs, mummification, and art.
Ancient Greece was made of many city-states, like Athens and Sparta.
In Athens, citizens voted on laws themselves.
This was an early kind of democracy.
The Greeks started the Olympic Games and built beautiful temples like the Parthenon.
Greek thinkers asked big questions about life, numbers, and nature.
Greek civilization was organized into independent city-states, each called a polis, sharing a language, religion, and the Olympic Games, traditionally dated to 776 BCE.

Athens developed a direct democracy in which adult male citizens debated and voted in the Assembly, especially after the reforms of Cleisthenes around 508 BCE; women, enslaved people, and foreigners were excluded.
Sparta, by contrast, was a military state ruled by two kings and a council of elders.
United, the Greeks turned back Persian invasions at Marathon (490 BCE) and Salamis (480 BCE).
Under Pericles, Athens built the Parthenon, completed in 432 BCE.

Philosophers Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle, historians Herodotus and Thucydides, and mathematicians such as Euclid and Pythagoras shaped later science and political thought, including the American founders' ideas about citizenship and mixed government.
The Bill of Rights is a list of freedoms that belong to every person in the United States.
It is the first ten changes, called amendments, added to the Constitution in 1791.
It protects the freedom to speak, to practice your religion, to gather peacefully, and to have a fair trial.
Many people would only agree to the Constitution if these rights were written down, so they could never be taken away easily.
When the Constitution was sent to the states, Anti-Federalists objected that it lacked a written guarantee of individual liberties.
James Madison drafted amendments in the First Congress in 1789, drawing on state declarations such as Virginia's Declaration of Rights of 1776.
Ten of the proposed amendments were ratified on December 15, 1791.

The First Amendment protects religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition; the Second protects the right to keep and bear arms; the Fourth guards against unreasonable searches and seizures; the Fifth, Sixth, and Seventh secure due process, a speedy and public trial, and trial by jury; the Eighth bars cruel and unusual punishment; and the Ninth and Tenth state that rights and powers not listed remain with the people and the states.
Originally these limits applied only to the federal government.
After the Fourteenth Amendment of 1868, courts gradually applied most of them to the states, a process called incorporation.
All living things are made of tiny building blocks called cells.
Cells are so small you need a microscope to see them.
Some living things, like bacteria, are just one cell.
Your body has trillions of cells.
Different cells do different jobs, like carrying oxygen in your blood or helping you think.
Robert Hooke named cells in 1665 after viewing cork through a microscope, and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek soon observed living single-celled organisms.

Cell theory, developed in the 1830s by Matthias Schleiden, Theodor Schwann, and later Rudolf Virchow, states that all living things are made of cells, that the cell is the basic unit of life, and that cells come from existing cells.
Prokaryotic cells, such as bacteria, lack a nucleus; eukaryotic cells, found in plants, animals, and fungi, keep DNA in a nucleus and contain organelles.
Mitochondria release energy from food, ribosomes build proteins, and the cell membrane controls what enters and leaves.
Plant cells also have a cell wall, a large central vacuole, and chloroplasts for photosynthesis.
The Civil War was a war between the northern states, called the Union, and southern states that formed the Confederacy.
Abraham Lincoln was President of the Union.
The war lasted four years and many soldiers died.
The Union won in 1865, and the Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery.

Disputes over the spread of slavery into western territories deepened through the 1850s, and after Abraham Lincoln's election in 1860 eleven Southern states seceded to form the Confederate States of America.
War began when Confederate forces fired on Fort Sumter in April 1861.
Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation of January 1, 1863, declared enslaved people in Confederate-held areas free, and about 180,000 Black soldiers served in the Union army.
The Union victory at Gettysburg in July 1863, where Lincoln later gave the Gettysburg Address, and the capture of Vicksburg turned the war.
Lee surrendered to General Ulysses S.
Grant at Appomattox Court House in April 1865.
The Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendments that followed abolished slavery, defined citizenship and equal protection, and protected voting regardless of race.
Computers only understand two signals: on and off.
Each 1 or 0 is called a bit.
By putting many bits together, a computer can store numbers, letters, pictures, and sounds.
Everything you see on a screen is made of ones and zeros.
Digital computers represent information in binary, base two, because electronic switches called transistors have two reliable states.
Each binary place is worth twice the one to its right, so 1011 in binary means 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11.
A group of eight bits, a byte, can hold 256 different values.
Text is stored with codes such as ASCII and Unicode, which assign a number to every character; in ASCII, capital A is 65.
Images are grids of pixels whose colors are numbers, and sound is a series of numbered samples.
In 1945 John von Neumann described the stored-program design, in which instructions and data share the same memory, still the basis of most computers.
A modern processor contains billions of transistors and performs billions of operations each second.
The Constitution is the rule book for the United States.
In the summer of 1787, leaders from twelve states met in Philadelphia to write it.
It begins with the words "We the People," which means the power of the government comes from the people.
The Constitution sets up three parts of government so no one person or group gets too much power.
It can be changed, but only with a lot of agreement.
The Constitution was drafted at the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia between May and September 1787 and signed by 39 delegates on September 17.
It replaced the Articles of Confederation, which had left the national government too weak to raise money or settle disputes between states.

The document is organized into a Preamble and seven articles: Article I creates Congress, Article II the presidency, Article III the federal courts, and the remaining articles cover the states, the amendment process, federal supremacy, and ratification.
Nine states had to ratify it before it took effect; New Hampshire became the ninth in June 1788, and the new government began in 1789.
Twenty-seven amendments have been added since, the first ten of which form the Bill of Rights.
Its core ideas are popular sovereignty, separation of powers, checks and balances, and federalism, the sharing of power between the nation and the states.
Earth has seven big pieces of land called continents: Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America.
Earth also has five oceans: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, and Arctic.
The Pacific is the biggest and deepest ocean.
Water covers most of our planet.
About 71 percent of Earth's surface is covered by water.
Geographers usually recognize seven continents and five oceans.
Asia is the largest continent in both area and population, with about 60 percent of the world's people, and Australia is the smallest.
The Pacific Ocean is larger than all the land on Earth combined and holds the deepest point, the Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench, nearly 11,000 meters down.
The Southern Ocean around Antarctica was recognized by the International Hydrographic Organization in 2000 and by the National Geographic Society in 2021.
About 300 million years ago the continents were joined in a supercontinent called Pangaea, which broke apart through plate tectonics, and the continents are still moving today.
On July 4, 1776, leaders of the thirteen colonies agreed to a paper that said they were free from the king of Great Britain.
It is called the Declaration of Independence.
Thomas Jefferson wrote most of it.
It says that all people are created equal and have rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
We celebrate July 4 every year as Independence Day.
The Second Continental Congress voted for independence on July 2, 1776, and approved the final text of the Declaration on July 4.
A committee of five, including John Adams and Benjamin Franklin, chose Thomas Jefferson to write the draft.

The document has three parts: a statement of principles, that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed and that people may alter or abolish a government that destroys their rights; a long list of grievances against King George III; and the formal declaration that the colonies are free and independent states.
Its ideas drew on earlier writers on natural rights and on a long tradition holding that rulers are bound by law.
The Declaration did not itself create a government, but it stated the purpose a just government must serve, and it has been cited ever since by movements seeking equal rights.
Electricity is a kind of energy that makes lights glow and machines run.
It flows through wires like water through a pipe.
A complete path for electricity is called a circuit.
Electricity can come from power plants, batteries, wind, or sunlight.
Electricity can be dangerous, so never touch outlets or power lines.
Electricity is the behavior of electric charge.
Electrons carry negative charge, and when they move through a conductor such as copper they form an electric current, measured in amperes.
Voltage, measured in volts, is the push that drives current, and resistance, measured in ohms, opposes it; Ohm's law relates them as V = I × R.
In 1752 Benjamin Franklin's kite experiment in Philadelphia showed that lightning is electrical.
Alessandro Volta built the first battery in 1800, and Michael Faraday's discoveries in 1831 made electric generators possible.
Power plants and wind turbines use generators to turn motion into electricity, while solar panels convert sunlight directly using semiconductors.
Off-grid homes store solar or wind energy in batteries and use inverters to change direct current (DC) into the alternating current (AC) that most appliances use.
A fraction names part of a whole.
If you cut a pizza into 4 equal slices and eat 1, you ate one fourth, written 1/4.
The bottom number, the denominator, tells how many equal parts the whole has.
The top number, the numerator, tells how many parts you have.
Two fourths is the same as one half.
A fraction a/b represents a divided by b, where b is not zero.
Fractions that name the same amount, such as 1/2, 2/4, and 3/6, are equivalent; multiplying or dividing the numerator and denominator by the same number gives an equivalent fraction.
To add or subtract fractions, rewrite them with a common denominator: 1/3 + 1/4 = 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12.
To multiply, multiply numerators and denominators: 2/3 × 3/5 = 6/15 = 2/5.
To divide, multiply by the reciprocal: 1/2 ÷ 1/4 = 1/2 × 4/1 = 2.
A fraction is in simplest form when the numerator and denominator share no factor but 1.
Fractions can also be written as decimals and percents: 3/4 = 0.75 = 75 percent.
Gravity is a pull that keeps your feet on the ground.
When you drop a ball, gravity pulls it down to Earth.
Gravity also keeps the Moon going around Earth and Earth going around the Sun.
The Moon's gravity is weaker than Earth's, so astronauts bounce there.
Gravity is the attraction between objects with mass.

In his Principia of 1687, Isaac Newton stated the law of universal gravitation: the force between two masses is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
Near Earth's surface, objects accelerate downward at about 9.8 meters per second squared, regardless of their mass when air resistance is ignored, as Galileo had argued.
Weight is the force of gravity on a mass, so a person weighs about one-sixth as much on the Moon.

In 1915 Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity described gravity as the curving of space and time by mass and energy, which explains effects Newton's law cannot, such as the bending of starlight around the Sun.
Gravity shapes tides, holds galaxies together, and keeps satellites in orbit.
A bill is an idea for a new law.
A member of Congress writes it down and introduces it.
First a small group called a committee studies it.
Then the House and the Senate each vote on it.
If both say yes, the bill goes to the President.
If the President signs it, it becomes a law.
A bill may be introduced in either chamber, though bills to raise revenue must start in the House.
It is referred to a committee, which can hold hearings, amend it in a markup session, and report it to the full chamber, or let it die.
After debate and a floor vote, the bill goes to the other chamber, which must pass the identical text; differences are settled by a conference committee or by passing amendments back and forth.
The President then has ten days, not counting Sundays, to sign or veto it.
If Congress is in session and the President does nothing, it becomes law without a signature; if Congress has adjourned, an unsigned bill dies, which is called a pocket veto.
A veto can be overridden by a two-thirds vote of both houses.
Compression means making information take up less space.
Instead, you could give "the" a short number and write the number each time.
Computers do this with repeated words and patterns.
Alexandria gives every sentence a number, so a sentence that appears many times is only stored once.
Lossless compression shrinks data so it can be restored exactly; lossy compression, used for photos and music, throws away detail people are unlikely to notice.
Run-length encoding replaces repeats like AAAAA with 5A.
Huffman coding (1952) gives common symbols shorter codes.
Dictionary methods, beginning with Lempel and Ziv's LZ77 in 1977, replace repeated strings with references to earlier copies, the idea behind ZIP files.

Alexandria's COG system works at a larger scale: every word and space gets a number, every distinct sentence gets a number made of a meaning number and a variant number, such as 1297.1, and each document becomes a sequence of sentence numbers.
A sentence that appears in a thousand documents is stored once and referenced a thousand times, and the number sequences can be fed directly to language models as tokens.
A paragraph is a group of sentences about one idea.
It starts with a topic sentence that tells the main idea.
Next come detail sentences that explain or give examples.
It ends with a closing sentence that wraps up the idea.
A strong paragraph develops one controlling idea.
The topic sentence states that idea and often sets up how it will be supported.
Supporting sentences provide evidence, examples, facts, or reasoning, and good writers explain how each piece of evidence connects to the main idea rather than simply listing facts.
Transitions such as for example, however, and as a result guide the reader between sentences.
A concluding sentence restates the idea in new words or links it to the next paragraph.
When writing from sources, a paragraph should cite where evidence comes from, quote sparingly, and put most information in the writer's own words.
Revising for unity, removing sentences that stray from the topic, and for coherence, making the order logical, turns a draft into a clear paragraph.
In 1804 Meriwether Lewis and William Clark set off from near St.
President Thomas Jefferson asked them to find a water route to the Pacific Ocean and to learn about the land, plants, and animals.
A Shoshone woman named Sacagawea helped them as a guide and interpreter.
They reached the Pacific in 1805 and came home in 1806.
After the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 doubled the size of the United States, Jefferson sent the Corps of Discovery under Lewis and Clark to map the Missouri River and seek a route to the Pacific.

The party of about thirty-three left Camp Dubois in May 1804, wintered among the Mandan and Hidatsa in present-day North Dakota, and crossed the Rocky Mountains with horses obtained from the Shoshone.
Sacagawea, traveling with her infant son, helped with language and relations with Native nations.
The expedition reached the Pacific coast in November 1805, built Fort Clatsop near the mouth of the Columbia River, and returned to St.
Their journals described more than 170 plants and 120 animals new to science and recorded meetings with dozens of Native nations, though they found no all-water route across the continent.
The Library of Congress is the biggest library in the world.
It holds millions of books, maps, photographs, letters, and recordings.
The people paid for it with their taxes, so it is held in trust for them.
Many of its collections can be read for free, and Alexandria brings some of them to you.
The Library of Congress was established in 1800 when the capital moved to Washington.
British troops burned the Capitol and the library's 3,000 volumes in 1814, and Thomas Jefferson sold his personal library of 6,487 books to restart it in 1815.
An 1870 copyright law required two copies of every copyrighted work to be deposited there, which helped it grow into the largest library in the world, with well over 170 million items.
Its collections include the papers of many presidents, the United States Reports, historic newspapers, maps, music, and recorded sound.
Paid for by taxpayers, the Library is a taxpayer trust: held in trust for the people who paid for it.
Much of it is digitized and free to read online, and Digital Alexandria stores those public texts as COG numbered sentences.
A map is a drawing of a place seen from above.
Maps have a compass rose that shows north, south, east, and west, and a key that explains the symbols.
Lines on a globe help us find places.
Lines that go around Earth like belts are latitude.
Lines that run from pole to pole are longitude.
Together they give every place on Earth its own address.
Latitude measures distance north or south of the equator, from 0° to 90°; longitude measures distance east or west of the prime meridian at Greenwich, England, from 0° to 180°.
A location such as 38.89° N, 77.00° W pinpoints the U.S.
Because Earth is round, no flat map can show it without distortion.
The Mercator projection, published by Gerardus Mercator in 1569, keeps compass directions true for navigation but greatly enlarges areas near the poles, making Greenland look as large as Africa.
Other projections preserve area or balance several kinds of distortion.
Map scale relates distance on a map to distance on the ground, such as 1:24,000.
Today GPS satellites let receivers compute latitude and longitude within meters, and geographic information systems layer data on digital maps.
A noun names a person, place, or thing, like dog or school.
A verb shows action or being, like run or is.
An adjective describes a noun, like big or blue.
In the sentence "The happy dog runs," dog is a noun, runs is a verb, and happy is an adjective.
English grammar traditionally recognizes eight parts of speech.
Nouns name people, places, things, and ideas; pronouns such as she and they stand in for nouns.
Verbs express action or state of being and carry tense.
Adjectives modify nouns and pronouns, and adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs, often answering how, when, or where.
Prepositions such as under and between show relationships, conjunctions such as and, but, and because join words and clauses, and interjections such as wow express emotion.
Many words change part of speech with use: in "a light rain" light is an adjective, but in "light the lamp" it is a verb.
Knowing the parts of speech helps writers build clear sentences, punctuate correctly, and understand how meaning is put together.
Plants make their own food using sunlight.
Leaves take in a gas from the air called carbon dioxide.
A green material in leaves, called chlorophyll, catches sunlight.
The plant uses this energy to make sugar for food, and it gives off oxygen, which people and animals breathe.
Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy.
The overall equation is 6CO2 + 6H2O + light energy → C6H12O6 + 6O2.
It takes place in chloroplasts, where the pigment chlorophyll absorbs mostly red and blue light and reflects green.
In the light-dependent reactions, on the thylakoid membranes, water is split, releasing oxygen and producing the energy carriers ATP and NADPH.
In the Calvin cycle, in the stroma, the enzyme RuBisCO fixes carbon dioxide into sugars using that ATP and NADPH.
In 1779 Jan Ingenhousz showed that plants produce oxygen only in light.
Photosynthesis supplies nearly all the oxygen in the atmosphere and the energy at the base of most food chains.
In the number 352, each digit has a place.
The 2 is in the ones place, the 5 is in the tens place, and the 3 is in the hundreds place.
So 352 means 3 hundreds, 5 tens, and 2 ones.
The same digit can be worth different amounts depending on where it sits.
Our number system is a positional, base-ten system: each place is worth ten times the place to its right.
In 4,072 the digits stand for 4 × 1,000 + 0 × 100 + 7 × 10 + 2 × 1, which is called expanded form.
The digit zero is essential as a placeholder; without it, 4,072 and 472 could not be told apart.

The Hindu-Arabic numerals and place-value system developed in India by about the 5th century, spread through the Islamic world, and reached Europe in the 1200s, helped by Fibonacci's Liber Abaci (1202).
Place value extends to the right of the decimal point, where places are tenths, hundredths, and thousandths.
Other bases work the same way: computers use base two, where each place is worth twice the one to its right.
The ground under our feet seems still, but it moves very slowly.
Earth's outer layer is broken into giant pieces called plates.
They move about as fast as your fingernails grow.
When plates bump, pull apart, or slide past each other, they can cause earthquakes and volcanoes and build mountains.
In 1912 Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift, noting that continents fit together like puzzle pieces and share matching fossils and rocks, but he could not explain what moved them.
In the 1950s and 1960s, mapping of the ocean floor revealed mid-ocean ridges and symmetrical magnetic stripes, evidence of seafloor spreading, and the theory of plate tectonics followed.
Earth's lithosphere is divided into seven or eight large plates and many smaller ones, riding on the softer asthenosphere.
At divergent boundaries, such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge running through Iceland, plates move apart and new crust forms.
At convergent boundaries plates collide: ocean crust subducts beneath other plates, forming trenches and volcanoes, or continents crumple into mountains like the Himalayas.
At transform boundaries, such as the San Andreas Fault, plates slide past each other.
Plates move a few centimeters per year.
Before the printing press, books were copied by hand, which took a very long time.
Around 1440, Johannes Gutenberg in Germany built a printing press with metal letters that could be moved and used again.
Now many copies of a book could be made quickly.
More people could buy books and learn to read.

Johannes Gutenberg of Mainz combined several inventions around 1440: individual metal type cast in a hand mold, an oil-based ink that stuck to metal, and a screw press adapted from wine and paper making.
His Bible, printed around 1455, showed that a press could match the quality of hand copying at a fraction of the cost.
Within fifty years presses operated in more than two hundred European cities and had produced millions of books.
Printing standardized spelling and texts, made scholarship easier to check and build upon, and allowed ideas to spread faster than authorities could control them.
Reformers such as Martin Luther used pamphlets to reach wide audiences, and printed books fed the Scientific Revolution.
Earlier, Chinese and Korean printers had used woodblocks and movable type, but the alphabet's small number of letters made Gutenberg's metal type especially efficient.
In 1517 a monk and teacher named Martin Luther wrote 95 points, called theses, asking the church to change some of its practices.
The printing press spread his ideas quickly.
Many people formed new churches, called Protestant churches.
Other reformers, like John Calvin and John Knox, also taught new ideas.
This time is called the Reformation.
The Reformation is usually dated to October 31, 1517, when Martin Luther posted his Ninety-five Theses in Wittenberg challenging the sale of indulgences.
Luther taught that salvation comes through faith and that Scripture is the highest authority, and he translated the Bible into German so ordinary people could read it.
John Calvin in Geneva and Huldrych Zwingli in Zurich led a Reformed branch; John Knox carried Reformed teaching to Scotland.

Reformers and their followers also argued about the limits of rulers' power: Scottish writers such as George Buchanan and Samuel Rutherford, in Lex, Rex (1644), argued that the king is under the law, ideas later read by American founders including John Witherspoon, a Scottish-born minister who signed the Declaration of Independence.
The Catholic Church answered with its own reforms at the Council of Trent, and Europe was divided by religious wars until the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.
A right triangle has one square corner, like the corner of a book.
If you know two sides of a right triangle, you can find the third using a special rule: a × a + b × b = c × c.
The side c is the longest side, across from the square corner.
For a triangle with sides 3 and 4, the long side is 5, because 9 + 16 = 25.
The Pythagorean theorem states that in a right triangle with legs a and b and hypotenuse c, a² + b² = c².
It is named for the Greek mathematician Pythagoras of Samos, who lived around 570 to 495 BCE, though Babylonian tablets show the relationship was known more than a thousand years earlier.
Euclid gave a famous proof in his Elements, and hundreds of proofs are known today.
Whole-number solutions such as 3-4-5 and 5-12-13 are called Pythagorean triples; builders have long used a 3-4-5 rope to make square corners.
The theorem underlies the distance formula in coordinate geometry, d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²), and is used in surveying, navigation, construction, and computer graphics.
Citizens have rights, which are freedoms that are protected, like speaking your mind and practicing your faith.
Citizens also have responsibilities, which are things they should do to help everyone.
Obeying laws, voting, serving on a jury, and helping your community are responsibilities.
Rights and responsibilities go together, like two sides of a coin.
Citizenship in the United States comes by birth on its soil or to citizen parents, or through naturalization, as set out in the Fourteenth Amendment's citizenship clause of 1868.
Constitutional rights include the freedoms of the First Amendment, the right to keep and bear arms, protection against unreasonable searches, due process, and equal protection of the laws.
Some duties are required by law: obeying federal, state, and local laws, paying taxes, serving on a jury when summoned, and registering with Selective Service for young men.
Others are civic responsibilities that keep self-government alive: staying informed, voting, respecting the rights of others, and taking part in the community.
Because the government draws its power from the people, the quality of a republic depends on how well its citizens use both their rights and their responsibilities.
Rivers are like roads made of water.
Long ago people traveled and traded on them.
The Mississippi River is one of the longest rivers in North America.
It flows south to the Gulf of Mexico.
The Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon over millions of years.
Rivers give water for farms, towns, and animals.
North America's largest river system, the Mississippi-Missouri, drains about 40 percent of the contiguous United States.
The Missouri, longer than the Mississippi itself, joins it near St.
Louis, and the Ohio joins at Cairo, Illinois.
Control of New Orleans at the Mississippi's mouth was a major reason for the Louisiana Purchase of 1803.

The Colorado River, flowing from the Rocky Mountains to the Gulf of California, cut the Grand Canyon and today supplies water to about 40 million people across seven U.S. states and Mexico, managed under the Colorado River Compact of 1922.
Lawrence links the Great Lakes to the Atlantic, the Columbia carried Lewis and Clark to the Pacific, and the Rio Grande forms part of the U.S.-Mexico border.
Rivers shaped where cities grew, powered early mills, and remain vital for irrigation, shipping, and hydroelectric power.
Long ago, the people of Rome got rid of their king and made a republic.
In a republic, people choose leaders to make decisions for them.
Rome had a Senate and two leaders called consuls who served for one year.
Romans wrote down their laws so everyone could know them.
Later, Rome was ruled by emperors.
According to tradition, Romans expelled their last king in 509 BCE and created a republic.
Two consuls, elected each year, held executive power and could check each other, while the Senate advised on policy and finances and popular assemblies passed laws and elected magistrates.
Conflict between patricians and plebeians produced the Twelve Tables, Rome's first written laws, around 450 BCE, and the office of tribune to protect common citizens.
Rome expanded across Italy and, after the Punic Wars with Carthage, around the Mediterranean.
Civil wars in the first century BCE weakened the republic; Julius Caesar was named dictator and assassinated in 44 BCE, and in 27 BCE Augustus became the first emperor.
The idea of a republic with separated offices, term limits, and written law strongly influenced the framers of the Constitution.
Our solar system is the Sun and everything that travels around it.
There are eight planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.
Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only one we know has life.
Gravity from the Sun keeps all the planets in their paths, called orbits.
The solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust.
The Sun holds more than 99.8 percent of its mass.
The four inner planets, Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, are small and rocky; the outer four are giants, Jupiter and Saturn made mostly of hydrogen and helium, and Uranus and Neptune rich in ices.
Between Mars and Jupiter lies the asteroid belt, and beyond Neptune the Kuiper Belt holds icy bodies including the dwarf planet Pluto, reclassified in 2006.
Planets follow elliptical orbits, as Johannes Kepler showed, and Isaac Newton explained them with the law of universal gravitation.
In 1610 Galileo's telescope revealed four moons orbiting Jupiter, strong evidence that not everything circles Earth.
Light from the Sun takes about eight minutes to reach Earth, which lies about 150 million kilometers away, a distance called one astronomical unit.
Everything around you is made of matter.
Matter can be a solid, a liquid, or a gas.
A solid, like ice, keeps its shape.
A liquid, like water, takes the shape of its container.
A gas, like steam, spreads out to fill any space.
Heating and cooling can change matter from one state to another, like ice melting into water.
The state of matter depends on how strongly particles are held together and how fast they move.
In solids, particles vibrate in fixed positions, giving a definite shape and volume.
In liquids, particles slide past one another, so volume is fixed but shape is not.
In gases, particles move freely and far apart, filling any container.
Plasma, an ionized gas found in stars and lightning, is often called the fourth state.
Changes of state include melting, freezing, evaporation and boiling, condensation, and sublimation, in which a solid becomes a gas directly, as dry ice does.
At sea level pure water freezes at 0 °C (32 °F) and boils at 100 °C (212 °F).
During a change of state, added heat goes into breaking bonds between particles rather than raising temperature, which is why ice water stays at 0 °C until the ice melts.
The Supreme Court is the top court in the United States.
Nine judges, called justices, sit on it.
When people disagree about what the Constitution means, the Supreme Court can make the final decision.
The justices listen to both sides, ask questions, and then vote.
They write down their reasons so everyone can read them.
Article III of the Constitution creates the Supreme Court, and the Judiciary Act of 1789 organized it; it first met in 1790.
Congress sets the number of justices, which has been nine since 1869.
Justices are nominated by the President, confirmed by the Senate, and serve during good behavior, usually for life.
Madison (1803), Chief Justice John Marshall explained the power of judicial review: courts may refuse to apply a law that conflicts with the Constitution.
Most cases reach the Court on appeal, and it chooses only a small share of the petitions it receives each year.
Decisions are explained in written opinions, including majority, concurring, and dissenting opinions.
Its rulings are collected in the United States Reports, one of the collections held in the Library of Congress.
Long ago, people from England and other countries came across the ocean to live in North America.
They built thirteen colonies along the Atlantic coast, from New Hampshire in the north to Georgia in the south.
People farmed, fished, built ships, and traded.
Many Native American nations already lived on this land.
In 1776 the thirteen colonies decided to become a new country, the United States.
English settlement began at Jamestown, Virginia, in 1607 and grew until Georgia, the last of the thirteen, was founded in 1732.
Historians group the colonies into three regions.
New England (Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Connecticut, Rhode Island) relied on fishing, shipbuilding, and trade.
The Middle Colonies (New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware) grew grain and were known for religious and ethnic variety.
The Southern Colonies (Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia) built plantation economies based on tobacco, rice, and indigo and on the labor of enslaved Africans.
Colonists governed themselves through elected assemblies such as Virginia's House of Burgesses, which first met in 1619.
That habit of self-government made new British taxes after 1763 feel like an attack on their rights, setting the stage for revolution.
The United States government has three parts, called branches.
The legislative branch, Congress, makes the laws.
The executive branch, led by the President, carries out the laws.
The judicial branch, the courts, decides what the laws mean.
Each branch can stop the others from doing too much.
This is called checks and balances.
The Constitution divides federal power among three branches, an idea the framers took from writers such as Montesquieu.
Congress, made up of the Senate and the House of Representatives, writes laws, sets taxes, and declares war.
The President enforces laws, commands the armed forces, and conducts foreign policy, with cabinet departments carrying out the daily work.
The Supreme Court and lower federal courts decide cases and controversies arising under the Constitution and federal law.

Checks and balances tie the branches together: the President can veto bills, Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses, the Senate confirms judges and approves treaties, Congress can impeach and remove officials, and courts can review whether laws and actions are constitutional.
The design aims to make government strong enough to act but divided enough that no one part can rule alone.
Voting is how people choose their leaders.
In the United States, citizens who are 18 or older can vote.
Each vote is secret, so you can choose freely.
People vote for the President, members of Congress, governors, mayors, and even school boards.
Long ago, many people were not allowed to vote.
Over time, laws and amendments gave more people that right.
The original Constitution left voting rules mostly to the states, and early on many states limited voting to adult white men who owned property.

Amendments steadily widened the franchise: the Fifteenth (1870) barred denying the vote because of race, the Nineteenth (1920) because of sex, the Twenty-fourth (1964) banned poll taxes in federal elections, and the Twenty-sixth (1971) set the voting age at eighteen.
The Voting Rights Act of 1965 enforced these guarantees against literacy tests and other barriers.

Presidents are chosen through the Electoral College, in which each state's electors equal its number of senators and representatives; members of Congress are elected directly, senators since the Seventeenth Amendment of 1913.
Elections are run by states and counties, which register voters, set polling places, and count ballots.
Water on Earth moves around and around in a cycle.
The Sun warms water in oceans and lakes, and it rises into the air as an invisible gas.
High in the sky the gas cools and forms tiny drops that make clouds.
When drops get heavy they fall as rain or snow.
The water collects in rivers and oceans, and the cycle starts again.
The water cycle, or hydrologic cycle, is powered by solar energy and gravity.
Evaporation from oceans supplies most atmospheric water vapor, joined by transpiration from plants; together these are called evapotranspiration.
As moist air rises it expands and cools; when it reaches its dew point, vapor condenses onto tiny particles to form clouds.
Droplets or ice crystals grow until they fall as precipitation.
On land, water runs off into streams and rivers, soaks into soil, or infiltrates to recharge groundwater in aquifers, and some is stored for long periods in glaciers and ice sheets.
About 97 percent of Earth's water is salty ocean water; most fresh water is locked in ice or underground, so the cycle's renewal of fresh water is vital for life and farming.
